title: Long-Term Agent Memory through Complementary Curation and Consolidation

paper.title: Long-Term Agent Memory through Complementary Curation and Consolidation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-horizon dialogue agents require effective memory systems to recall facts, events, and relationships
from interaction histories. In this work, we propose a hybrid-memory architecture comprising episodic memories and structured relational memories and a consolidation mechanism which improves efficiency.
We conduct an empirical study across two benchmarks:
LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S.
Our experiments demonstrate that the two memory types are consistently
complementary, combining both outperforms state-of-the-art memory frameworks and achieves 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agentic capability of sustaining multi-turn interactions Wang et al. (2024) ; Hu et al. (2025) . However, their ability to recall, integrate, and reason over long interaction histories remains fundamentally limited. These limitations have motivated the development of long-term memory systems that explicitly store and retrieve learning from past interactions Zhang et al. (2025) . By enabling selective access to historical experience, these mechanisms mitigate the need for massive context windows, fostering more coherent and efficient agent behavior. Prior work on agentic memories can be primarily categorized into two types. Parametric memory Wei et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) embeds knowledge directly into model parameters through training, enabling low-latency inference; however, encoding is computationally expensive, frequent updates are infeasible, and unconstrained modifications may induce hallucination. In contrast, non-parametric memory Chhikara et al. (2025) ; Rasmussen et al. (2025) ; Nan et al. (2025) leverages external memory systems that store and retrieve information on demand, offering scalability and adaptability without training, though at the expense of additional retrieval latency. In this work, we focus on the latter approach, and propose a hybrid memory system of episodic memory which stores distinct events from the interactions, preserving the temporal ordering and contextual richness, and structured relational memory which extracts entity specific tuples from dialogues, making implicit connections between people, places, and facts explicit and enabling relational inference across sessions. These two representations reflect fundamentally different assumptions about what makes memory useful: episodic memory preserves narrative context and sequence , while structured relational memory prioritizes compact, queryable relational structure . Furthermore, we introduce an offline memory consolidation mechanism that selectively merges related or redundant memories and removes conflicting or outdated entries, enabling scalable and efficient long-term memory management. We evaluate our system on two long-horizon dialogue benchmarks, LoCoMo Maharana et al. (2024) and LongMemEval-S Wu et al. (2025) . Our empirical results demonstrate that episodic and structured relational memory together deliver strong empirical performance, with our hybrid system outperforming state-of-the-art baseline methods on both benchmarks. Our memory consolidation method further shows effective compression of the memory store by 16.34% without much loss in performance. Moreover, on the LoCoMo benchmark, the consolidated system improves accuracy on both single-hop and multi-hop QA tasks. Figure 1: Architecture Overview. Stage 1 (Memory Curation): The Episodic Memory Manager stores timestamped summaries, while the Relational Memory Manager extracts structured knowledge triplets with conversational context. Stage 2 (Consolidation): Memory entries are clustered based on semantic similarity, with memories merged or deleted to maintain efficiency. Stage 3 (Memory Retrieval and QA): Given a user query, relevant memories are retrieved from both episodic and relational stores to generate contextually grounded responses.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Recent work on long-term memory includes virtual context management : MemoryOS Kang et al. (2025) , MemGPT Packer et al. (2023) , and ReadAgent Lee et al. (2024) page information between a context window and external storage to handle inputs that exceed the model’s attention span. A second line of work extracts and maintains salient content across sessions: Mem0 Chhikara et al. (2025) applies per-turn CRUD operations over extracted facts, A-Mem Xu et al. (2026) organizes memories as evolving Zettelkasten notes with adaptive linking, and H-Mem Sun and Zeng (2025) adds hierarchical indexing for scalable routing. Zep Rasmussen et al. (2025) builds a temporal graph to support structured multi-hop traversal, while Nemori Nan et al. (2025) forms coherent episodes through adaptive distillation. Our work differs in two ways. First, we combine episodic memory with a lightweight relational tuple store retrieved by semantic similarity and grounded with timestamps and source context, leveraging complementary narrative and entity-relation memories. Second, our offline consolidation phase merges redundant memories, improving efficiency without much loss in accuracy. A detailed comparison is provided in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Hybrid memory operates in three phases: an offline curation phase that processes each conversation session, an offline consolidation phase, and a final retrieval-and-generation phase that responds to user queries. Figure 1 presents an overview of our proposed memory system.

sections.heading: 3.1 Memory Curation
sections.text: Both memory stores are populated at session granularity: after each conversation session concludes, we run curation over its transcript.

sections.heading: Episodic Memory.
sections.text: For each session, we create holistic episodic memories using an LLM. As shown in Figure 1 , each entry contains three fields: a short title identifying the episode, a one-sentence summary distilling its key point, and a details paragraph preserving the narrative context, including the event and any relevant background. Each episodic record is additionally annotated with the session timestamp. The prompt for episodic memory curation is shown in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Structured Relational Memory.
sections.text: We observe that conversations naturally express persistent facts about entities and their relationships, including who someone is, what they do, who they are connected to. These relationships are better represented as structured relational tuples. To this end, we prompt an LLM to extract entity-relation tuples from the dialogues. Each tuple is stored as ( e , r , o , t , c ) (e,\,r,\,o,\,t,\,c) . As shown in Figure 1 , e e is the entity , r r the relation label , o o the object , t t the timestamp , and c c the source context which captures the richer context from which the tuple was extracted. The contextual description c c provides provenance: it records not just what the tuple asserts but in what context it was mentioned, which is important for preserving nuance that structured extraction inevitably loses, such as the speaker’s intent, the circumstances under which a fact was stated, and additional details. The timestamp t t additionally grounds each triplet temporally, addressing a common failure mode of relation-based memory where relational facts are stored without any record of when they were true. sections.heading: 3.2 Memory Consolidation
sections.text: As interactions accumulate, the memory store grows monotonically, increasing storage costs, retrieval overhead, and introduction of noise. To address this, we introduce a periodic clustering-based consolidation mechanism that groups semantically similar memories using HDBSCAN Campello et al. (2013) , enabling the merging of evolving concepts, resolution of conflicting information, and de-duplication of redundant entries across sessions. As shown in Figure 1 , all memories in a cluster are fed to an LLM which then decides whether to merge or delete memories. sections.heading: 3.3 Memory Retrieval & Question Answering
sections.text: At query time, we perform independent top- k k semantic similarity searches over the episodic memory and structured relational memory stores separately. For episodic memory, each episode’s details field is indexed, yielding one vector per episode. For structured relational memory, each tuple is indexed as a natural-language string concatenating its components (e.g., “Subject, Relation, Object” ), yielding one vector per triplet. The two stores are searched independently, returning the top- k k episodes from episodic memory and the top- 2 ​ k 2k tuples from structured relational memory. The episodic memories are more verbose than relational tuples, so within the same budget approximately twice as many relational entries can be retrieved. sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate our framework on two long-horizon dialogue benchmarks: LoCoMo Maharana et al. (2024) , featuring 1,540 QA pairs from 10 distinct dialogues across four reasoning categories: Single-Hop , Multi-Hop , Temporal , and Open-domain . On average, the conversations in LoCoMo span multiple sessions with 24K tokens; and LongMemEval-S Wu et al. (2025) , a substantially more challenging evaluation setting, comprising 500 meticulously curated questions embedded within synthetic but realistic chat histories that average 115K tokens per question.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare with state-of-the-art memory frameworks, including FullContext (all sessions placed in context) RAG-4096 (sessions chunked into 4096 token segments), LangMem Chase (2022) , Mem0 Chhikara et al. (2025) , Zep Rasmussen et al. (2025) , and Nemori Nan et al. (2025) .

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: We report results where memory curation, consolidation and answer generation are backed by gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-4o-mini models. We use text-embedding-3-small for vector embedding and retrieval. For clustering we have used UMAP McInnes et al. (2018) for dimension reduction and density based HDBSCAN Campello et al. (2013) for clustering. Detailed hyperparameters are in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Main Results.
sections.text: Table 1 shows the performance on the LoCoMo benchmark. Our system consistently outperforms all baselines when using gpt-4o-mini , achieving a score of 83.5 % 83.5\% . Notably, this surpasses the FullContext baseline, empirically validating that the addition of long context can lead to performance degradation. With gpt-4.1-mini , our approach reaches 90.2 % 90.2\% , a significant 6.7 % 6.7\% absolute improvement over the gpt-4o-mini results. While this score is slightly below the FullContext performance of 91.3 % 91.3\% , our system remains highly competitive while utilizing 87 % 87\% fewer tokens. The most significant gains are observed in Multi-Hop and Temporal reasoning tasks, which directly reflect the strengths of our dual-memory setup. Episodic memory preserves interactions as a timestamped timeline, allowing the model to track the order of events for temporal questions. Meanwhile, structured relational memories capture complex entity-relation dependencies, facilitating effective multi-hop inference over distinct facts. Appendix D provides an ablation study on the contribution of each component. The results demonstrate that the most substantial improvements (+6.3 points in Multi-Hop and +6.8 points in Temporal reasoning on gpt-4o-mini ) emerge due to interaction between the two memory types. Table 2 presents the results for the LongMemEval-S benchmark. Our method attains an overall score of 85.5 % 85.5\% , consistently surpassing both the FullContext baseline and Nemori across nearly all evaluation categories.

sections.heading: Efficiency.
sections.text: In Table 3 , we compare our system against the baselines in terms of the average number of tokens consumed per question. Our approach uses comparable tokens to Nemori , while achieving a 9.1 9.1 point improvement in accuracy. Furthermore, as in Table 5 , our consolidation method reduces the size of the memory store by 16.34 % 16.34\% with only 1% degradation in performance, demonstrating effective memory compression without much loss in accuracy.

sections.heading: 5 Analysis and Ablations
sections.text: We analyse the sensitivity of the system to its two main hyperparameters and its robustness across backbone LLMs. The contribution of each individual memory type is reported in Appendix D . All experiments in this section use LoCoMo.

sections.text: We conduct a sensitivity analysis on the primary clustering hyperparameter, min_cluster_size (mcs), which controls the minimum number of memory points required to form a cluster. Performance is largely stable for mcs ∈ [ 5 , 20 ] \in[5,20] , with LLM Score ranging from 0.892–0.898, all within 1 point of the no-consolidation baseline (0.902). At mcs = 2 =2 , performance drops by 2.6 points, which we attribute to over-aggressive consolidation where small groups of similar embeddings are prematurely merged. As mcs increases, memory compression decreases monotonically from 30.9% to 9.6%, while the number of clusters (and corresponding LLM consolidation calls) is reduced by up to 15 × \times . This highlights a favorable trade-off: moderate cluster sizes (mcs ∈ [ 5 , 10 ] \in[5,10] ) achieve meaningful compression (16–22%) with negligible accuracy loss.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented a Hybrid memory system for agents that curates and retrieves both episodic memory and structured relational memory, and conducted an empirical study across LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S. Our results demonstrate strong performance combining both memory types, and improved efficiency with memory consolidation without much loss in performance.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: While our proposed memory system demonstrates strong performance, several areas remain for further refinement. First, our current evaluation focuses exclusively on textual conversational data. Although the system is modality agnostic, extending it to support non-textual modalities such as vision and audio remains an important direction for future work. Second, our experiments reveal that memory curation quality can vary substantially across different backbone LLMs, as observed shifting from gpt-4.1-mini to gpt-4o-mini resulted in a 6.7 percentage point drop. This sensitivity reflects a broader challenge faced by existing agentic memory systems, where memory curation and consolidation are inherently influenced by model-specific reasoning and representation biases. Developing memory mechanisms that are robust and consistent across diverse model families remains an open and important research problem.

sections.heading: Appendix A Prompt used for Episodic Memory Curation
sections.text: Role: You are an Episodic Memory Curator. Your job is to extract HOLISTIC episodes from conversations capturing complete narratives rather than fragmented facts. TASK: Extract CONSOLIDATED episodic memories from the conversation below. Focus on creating coherent, comprehensive episodes that capture the full context of events. Current Date: {session_date} CONVERSATION: {session_text} EXTRACTION RULES: 1. WHAT TO CAPTURE (be exhaustive): • Events: meetings, trips, celebrations, appointments, activities. • Plans and scheduled activities (with exact dates if mentioned). • Preferences, opinions, and subjective feelings (e.g., “X loves hiking”). • Biographical facts: family details, careers, hobbies, pets. • Specific quantities: counts, frequencies, durations. • Advice given, specific phrases, exact quotes worth remembering. • Relationships between people mentioned. • Past events mentioned (e.g., “last year we saw X”). • NOT: Casual greetings or meta-conversation. 2. TEMPORAL PRECISION (CRITICAL): • The “Current Date” is WHEN THIS CONVERSATION HAPPENED. • For relative expressions, show your arithmetic explicitly: – “last Saturday” → \rightarrow count back to most recent Saturday before Current Date. – “next month” → \rightarrow the calendar month after Current Date’s month. – “yesterday” → \rightarrow Current Date minus 1 day. • Use YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM, or YYYY format. If no info, use null. 3. DETAIL PRESERVATION (CRITICAL): • Capture EXACT names, numbers, places, titles, and species. • Preserve exact sentiments and verbatim frequencies. • Prefer granular episodes over fewer big ones. 4. MEDIA INFORMATION • Preserve full caption text; record visible text (signs, posters). • Describe specific objects, scenes, or people visible in the image. 5. OUTPUT FORMAT: Return a JSON array of objects with this exact structure: { "title": "Short descriptive title (3-7 words)", "summary": "One-sentence description", "details": "Concise specifics. Names, numbers, quotes.", "timestamp": "ISO date string (YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM, YYYY) or null" } OUTPUT JSON ONLY (No markdown, no explanations)

sections.heading: Appendix B Prompt used for Relational Memory Curation

Current Date: {session_date} CONVERSATION: {session_text} EXTRACTION RULES: 1. WHAT TO EXTRACT (be exhaustive) • Events: meetings, trips, celebrations, appointments, activities. • Plans and scheduled activities (with exact dates if mentioned). • Preferences, opinions, and subjective feelings (e.g., “X loves hiking”). • Biographical facts: family details, careers, hobbies, pets. • Specific quantities: counts, frequencies, durations. • Advice given, specific phrases, exact quotes worth remembering. • Relationships between people mentioned. • Past events mentioned (e.g., “last year we saw X”). • NOT: Casual greetings or meta-conversation. 2. sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation details
sections.text: The consolidation pipeline follows a two-phase architecture inspired by BERTopic Grootendorst (2022) . In the first phase, all stored memories with their pre-computed 1536-dimensional embeddings produced by OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model are projected into a lower-dimensional space using UMAP McInnes et al. (2018) with cosine distance, 10 neighbors, 5 target components, and minimum distance of zero. The reduced representations are then clustered using HDBSCAN Campello et al. (2013) with Euclidean distance, Excess of Mass cluster selection, minimum cluster size of 10, and minimum samples of 1.

sections.heading: Appendix E Extended Comparison with Prior Work
sections.text: Prior memory systems differ from ours along three axes: representation , curation strategy , and operational cost . We summarize the key contrasts below.

sections.heading: Representation.
sections.text: Zep Rasmussen et al. (2025) maintains a temporal knowledge graph with entity nodes, fact edges, and validity intervals, enabling graph traversal at the cost of entity resolution, edge deduplication, and conflict detection. A-Mem Xu et al. (2026) organizes memories as Zettelkasten-style notes with evolving links between entries, while H-Mem Sun and Zeng (2025) relies on hierarchical indexing for routing. In contrast, we use two complementary flat stores: episodic records that preserve narrative context and relational tuples retrieved by semantic similarity. This sacrifices native graph traversal but avoids the overhead of graph construction and hierarchy maintenance.

sections.heading: Curation strategy.
sections.text: Mem0 Chhikara et al. (2025) processes each turn individually with add/update/delete/no-op operations, which fragments inter-turn context. Nemori Nan et al. (2025) adaptively distills semantic knowledge based on prediction error against an anticipatory schema, focusing on what to store. Our method instead targets how memory should be represented: we perform a single session-level curation pass that produces episodic and relational entries, and we apply offline clustering-based consolidation to merge redundant memories and remove outdated ones.

sections.heading: Operational cost.
sections.text: Turnwise systems such as Mem0 and A-Mem scale LLM calls linearly with conversation length, and dynamic retrieval schemes incur additional LLM rounds at query time. Our session-level curation amortizes extraction across many turns, and a fixed top- k k retrieval avoids extra LLM calls. Consolidation runs offline and can be triggered infrequently (e.g., every 10-20 sessions), keeping long-horizon operation tractable while preserving QA accuracy.

In this work, we propose a hybrid-memory architecture comprising episodic memories and structured relational memories and a consolidation mechanism which improves efficiency. We conduct an empirical study across two benchmarks: LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S. Our experiments demonstrate that the two memory types are consistently complementary, combining both outperforms state-of-the-art memory frameworks and achieves 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S. 1 Introduction Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agentic capability of sustaining multi-turn interactions Wang et al. (2024) ; Hu et al. (2025) . However, their ability to recall, integrate, and reason over long interaction histories remains fundamentally limited. These limitations have motivated the development of long-term memory systems that explicitly store and retrieve learning from past interactions Zhang et al. (2025) . By enabling selective access to historical experience, these mechanisms mitigate the need for massive context windows, fostering more coherent and efficient agent behavior. Prior work on agentic memories can be primarily categorized into two types. Parametric memory Wei et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) embeds knowledge directly into model parameters through training, enabling low-latency inference; however, encoding is computationally expensive, frequent updates are infeasible, and unconstrained modifications may induce hallucination. In contrast, non-parametric memory Chhikara et al. (2025) ; Rasmussen et al. (2025) ; Nan et al. (2025) leverages external memory systems that store and retrieve information on demand, offering scalability and adaptability without training, though at the expense of additional retrieval latency. In this work, we focus on the latter approach, and propose a hybrid memory system of episodic memory which stores distinct events from the interactions, preserving the temporal ordering and contextual richness, and structured relational memory which extracts entity specific tuples from dialogues, making implicit connections between people, places, and facts explicit and enabling relational inference across sessions. These two representations reflect fundamentally different assumptions about what makes memory useful: episodic memory preserves narrative context and sequence , while structured relational memory prioritizes compact, queryable relational structure . Furthermore, we introduce an offline memory consolidation mechanism that selectively merges related or redundant memories and removes conflicting or outdated entries, enabling scalable and efficient long-term memory management. We evaluate our system on two long-horizon dialogue benchmarks, LoCoMo Maharana et al. (2024) and LongMemEval-S Wu et al. (2025) . Our empirical results demonstrate that episodic and structured relational memory together deliver strong empirical performance, with our hybrid system outperforming state-of-the-art baseline methods on both benchmarks. Our memory consolidation method further shows effective compression of the memory store by 16.34% without much loss in performance. Moreover, on the LoCoMo benchmark, the consolidated system improves accuracy on both single-hop and multi-hop QA tasks. Figure 1: Architecture Overview. Stage 1 (Memory Curation): The Episodic Memory Manager stores timestamped summaries, while the Relational Memory Manager extracts structured knowledge triplets with conversational context. Stage 2 (Consolidation): Memory entries are clustered based on semantic similarity, with memories merged or deleted to maintain efficiency. Stage 3 (Memory Retrieval and QA): Given a user query, relevant memories are retrieved from both episodic and relational stores to generate contextually grounded responses. 2 Related Work Recent work on long-term memory includes virtual context management : MemoryOS Kang et al. (2025) , MemGPT Packer et al. (2023) , and ReadAgent Lee et al. (2024) page information between a context window and external storage to handle inputs that exceed the model’s attention span. A second line of work extracts and maintains salient content across sessions: Mem0 Chhikara et al. (2025) applies per-turn CRUD operations over extracted facts, A-Mem Xu et al. (2026) organizes memories as evolving Zettelkasten notes with adaptive linking, and H-Mem Sun and Zeng (2025) adds hierarchical indexing for scalable routing. Zep Rasmussen et al. (2025) builds a temporal graph to support structured multi-hop traversal, while Nemori Nan et al. (2025) forms coherent episodes through adaptive distillation. Our work differs in two ways. First, we combine episodic memory with a lightweight relational tuple store retrieved by semantic similarity and grounded with timestamps and source context, leveraging complementary narrative and entity-relation memories. Second, our offline consolidation phase merges redundant memories, improving efficiency without much loss in accuracy. A detailed comparison is provided in Appendix E . 3 Method Hybrid memory operates in three phases: an offline curation phase that processes each conversation session, an offline consolidation phase, and a final retrieval-and-generation phase that responds to user queries. Figure 1 presents an overview of our proposed memory system. 3.1 Memory Curation Both memory stores are populated at session granularity: after each conversation session concludes, we run curation over its transcript. Episodic Memory. For each session, we create holistic episodic memories using an LLM. As shown in Figure 1 , each entry contains three fields: a short title identifying the episode, a one-sentence summary distilling its key point, and a details paragraph preserving the narrative context, including the event and any relevant background. Each episodic record is additionally annotated with the session timestamp. The prompt for episodic memory curation is shown in Appendix A . Structured Relational Memory. We observe that conversations naturally express persistent facts about entities and their relationships, including who someone is, what they do, who they are connected to. These relationships are better represented as structured relational tuples. To this end, we prompt an LLM to extract entity-relation tuples from the dialogues. Each tuple is stored as ( e , r , o , t , c ) (e,\,r,\,o,\,t,\,c) . As shown in Figure 1 , e e is the entity , r r the relation label , o o the object , t t the timestamp , and c c the source context which captures the richer context from which the tuple was extracted. The contextual description c c provides provenance: it records not just what the tuple asserts but in what context it was mentioned, which is important for preserving nuance that structured extraction inevitably loses, such as the speaker’s intent, the circumstances under which a fact was stated, and additional details. The timestamp t t additionally grounds each triplet temporally, addressing a common failure mode of relation-based memory where relational facts are stored without any record of when they were true. To address this, we introduce a periodic clustering-based consolidation mechanism that groups semantically similar memories using HDBSCAN Campello et al. We compare with state-of-the-art memory frameworks, including FullContext (all sessions placed in context) RAG-4096 (sessions chunked into 4096 token segments), LangMem Chase (2022) , Mem0 Chhikara et al. (2025) , Zep Rasmussen et al. (2025) , and Nemori Nan et al. (2025) . Implementation. We report results where memory curation, consolidation and answer generation are backed by gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-4o-mini models. We use text-embedding-3-small for vector embedding and retrieval. For clustering we have used UMAP McInnes et al. (2018) for dimension reduction and density based HDBSCAN Campello et al. (2013) for clustering. Detailed hyperparameters are in Appendix C . 4.2 Results Main Results. Table 1 shows the performance on the LoCoMo benchmark. Our system consistently outperforms all baselines when using gpt-4o-mini , achieving a score of 83.5 % 83.5\% . Notably, this surpasses the FullContext baseline, empirically validating that the addition of long context can lead to performance degradation. With gpt-4.1-mini , our approach reaches 90.2 % 90.2\% , a significant 6.7 % 6.7\% absolute improvement over the gpt-4o-mini results. While this score is slightly below the FullContext performance of 91.3 % 91.3\% , our system remains highly competitive while utilizing 87 % 87\% fewer tokens. The most significant gains are observed in Multi-Hop and Temporal reasoning tasks, which directly reflect the strengths of our dual-memory setup. Episodic memory preserves interactions as a timestamped timeline, allowing the model to track the order of events for temporal questions. Meanwhile, structured relational memories capture complex entity-relation dependencies, facilitating effective multi-hop inference over distinct facts. Appendix D provides an ablation study on the contribution of each component. The results demonstrate that the most substantial improvements (+6.3 points in Multi-Hop and +6.8 points in Temporal reasoning on gpt-4o-mini ) emerge due to interaction between the two memory types. Table 2 presents the results for the LongMemEval-S benchmark. Our method attains an overall score of 85.5 % 85.5\% , consistently surpassing both the FullContext baseline and Nemori across nearly all evaluation categories. Efficiency. In Table 3 , we compare our system against the baselines in terms of the average number of tokens consumed per question. Our approach uses comparable tokens to Nemori , while achieving a 9.1 9.1 point improvement in accuracy. Furthermore, as in Table 5 , our consolidation method reduces the size of the memory store by 16.34 % 16.34\% with only 1% degradation in performance, demonstrating effective memory compression without much loss in accuracy. 5 Analysis and Ablations We analyse the sensitivity of the system to its two main hyperparameters and its robustness across backbone LLMs. The contribution of each individual memory type is reported in Appendix D . Our results demonstrate strong performance combining both memory types, and improved efficiency with memory consolidation without much loss in performance. 7 Limitations While our proposed memory system demonstrates strong performance, several areas remain for further refinement. First, our current evaluation focuses exclusively on textual conversational data. Although the system is modality agnostic, extending it to support non-textual modalities such as vision and audio remains an important direction for future work. Second, our experiments reveal that memory curation quality can vary substantially across different backbone LLMs, as observed shifting from gpt-4.1-mini to gpt-4o-mini resulted in a 6.7 percentage point drop. This sensitivity reflects a broader challenge faced by existing agentic memory systems, where memory curation and consolidation are inherently influenced by model-specific reasoning and representation biases. Appendix E Extended Comparison with Prior Work Prior memory systems differ from ours along three axes: representation , curation strategy , and operational cost . We summarize the key contrasts below. Representation. Zep Rasmussen et al. (2025) maintains a temporal knowledge graph with entity nodes, fact edges, and validity intervals, enabling graph traversal at the cost of entity resolution, edge deduplication, and conflict detection. A-Mem Xu et al. (2026) organizes memories as Zettelkasten-style notes with evolving links between entries, while H-Mem Sun and Zeng (2025) relies on hierarchical indexing for routing. In contrast, we use two complementary flat stores: episodic records that preserve narrative context and relational tuples retrieved by semantic similarity. This sacrifices native graph traversal but avoids the overhead of graph construction and hierarchy maintenance. Curation strategy. Mem0 Chhikara et al. (2025) processes each turn individually with add/update/delete/no-op operations, which fragments inter-turn context. Nemori Nan et al. (2025) adaptively distills semantic knowledge based on prediction error against an anticipatory schema, focusing on what to store. Our method instead targets how memory should be represented: we perform a single session-level curation pass that produces episodic and relational entries, and we apply offline clustering-based consolidation to merge redundant memories and remove outdated ones. Operational cost. Turnwise systems such as Mem0 and A-Mem scale LLM calls linearly with conversation length, and dynamic retrieval schemes incur additional LLM rounds at query time. Our session-level curation amortizes extraction across many turns, and a fixed top- k k retrieval avoids extra LLM calls. Consolidation runs offline and can be triggered infrequently (e.g., every 10-20 sessions), keeping long-horizon operation tractable while preserving QA accuracy.
